title: Simulation tools and simulating computer systems
subtitle: From Python to GPSS, and using simulation to design the very machines that run it.

sections.title: Simulation languages and tools
sections.body: You can write a simulator in any language — Java, Python (SimPy), C++ — but dedicated tools save effort. GPSS models a system as transactions flowing through blocks (GENERATE, QUEUE, SEIZE, ADVANCE, RELEASE, TERMINATE). Commercial packages (Arena, AnyLogic, Simulink) add graphical building and animation. Whatever the tool, the core is the same: a clock, an event list, random streams and statistics collectors.

choices.text: The entities moving through the system (customers, jobs, packets).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Blocks describe what happens to them.

sections.title: A queue simulator in code
sections.body: Even a few lines of C++ give a working model. This program simulates a single-server queue with a deterministic pattern (arrival every 3 units, service of 2 each) and prints each customer’s wait — run it and step through with the DSA Lab.

worked.why: Arrival every 3, service 2 ⇒ the server is free before each arrival.
Change the service time to 4: customer i starts at max(arrival, previous finish).

questions.prompt: Why is this model’s total wait 0?

choices.text: Service time 2 is less than the inter-arrival gap 3, so the server is always free.

figures.caption: Figure 9.2.1 — A queue simulator in code
figures.note: Service (2) is faster than arrivals (every 3), so nobody waits: total wait 0.

sections.title: CPU and memory simulation
sections.body: Computer architects evaluate designs before building them. A CPU simulator executes instructions and counts cycles; a memory simulator replays an address trace through a cache model. The scheduling chapter's Round Robin with quantum 4 yields an average wait of 5.67; a direct-mapped cache on the address trace 0 8 0 6 8 suffers 5 misses. Changing the parameters and re-running is exactly a simulation experiment.

questions.prompt: Trace-driven simulation of a cache replays…

choices.text: A recorded sequence of memory addresses through the cache model.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Changing cache parameters is then cheap.

sections.title: Network simulation
sections.body: Network simulators (ns-3, OMNeT++, Cisco Packet Tracer) model nodes, links, queues and protocols as discrete events: a packet arrives at a router, waits in a queue, is transmitted, propagates. A router output port is exactly an M/M/1-style queue: at ρ = 0.5 the simulated utilisation is 0.485 and the mean number in system 0.863.

questions.prompt: What kind of simulation are network simulators?

choices.text: Discrete-event: state changes at packet events.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The clock jumps between arrivals, transmissions and timeouts.

figures.caption: Figure 10.2.1 — a router output queue
figures.note: A router port as a queue.

problems.prompt: Why simulate a new cache design rather than build it?
problems.answer: Building hardware costs months and millions; a trace-driven simulator evaluates hit rate and AMAT for many sizes and policies in minutes and reveals the best design before any silicon is made.

sections.title: High-level system simulation
sections.body: Full-system simulators (gem5, QEMU) boot an operating system on a model of a computer, trading speed for detail — cycle-accurate is slowest. Choosing the abstraction level is the main design decision: the right model answers the question at the lowest cost.

choices.text: Usually slower, because it models more.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Pick the least detail that answers the question.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Simulation languages package the clock, event list, streams and statistics.
  • CPU, memory and network simulators are DES in disguise.
